Women shall not wear the clothing of strangers, and men shall not wear the clothing of relatives
Women shall not wear old clothing, and men shall not wear new clothing

content: According to Deuteronomy 23:21-23, if you VOW to the LORD — what?
explanation:
Deuteronomy 23:21-23 clearly teaches: 'When you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to fulfill it... you must be sure to do what you have vowed to the LORD.' Therefore, the correct answer is to fulfill it promptly, without delay.

Distractor 1 (close but incorrect) is wrong because this passage does not mention offering an additional sin offering for delay, but emphasizes not delaying from the start.
Distractor 2 is wrong because the commandment applies to all vows made to the LORD, not limited by location.
Distractor 3 reflects a common misunderstanding but is wrong, because verse 23 clearly states: 'you must be sure to do what you have vowed,' not allowing arbitrary substitution.
options: Must offer an additional sin offering if delayed
Only required to fulfill if vowed at the temple
FULFILL it without DELAY — for the LORD will require it of you; if you do NOT vow, NO sin
May substitute with an offering of equivalent value

content: According to Deuteronomy 24:14-15, regarding the POOR DAY-LABORER, the EMPLOYER must do what?
explanation: The question is based on Deuteronomy 24:14-15. The correct answer is 'Pay them their wages on the same day, before sunset' because verse 15 clearly states: 'You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets, for he is poor and his heart is set on it.' Distractor 1 ('Pay them their wages on the same day, before sunrise') is close but incorrect in a key detail (sunrise instead of sunset). Distractor 2 ('Pay them at the end of the week, before the day of rest') has the idea of a deadline but deviates from the specific 'on the same day' requirement of the question, and the Bible does not mention 'the end of the week' here. Distractor 3 ('Allow them to rest and provide them with food') describes a different humanitarian principle that can be found in nearby passages (such as laws about Sabbath rest or general treatment of the poor), but it is not the specific command about paying wages stated in Deuteronomy 24:14-15.
options: Pay them their wages on the same day, before sunrise
PAY WAGES the SAME DAY — do NOT let sun set on WAGES; the POOR depends on WAGES; if not, he CRIES to the LORD, you SIN
Pay them at the end of the week, before the day of rest
Allow them to rest and provide them with food

content: According to Deuteronomy 26:1-11, on entering the land, each brings FIRSTFRUITS — to where? Recites what?
explanation:
Deuteronomy 26:2-5 records: 'You shall take some of the first of all the fruit... and you shall go to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name to dwell there... And you shall declare...: "A wandering Aramean was my father... And the LORD brought us out of Egypt..."'. Therefore, the correct answer is right because it specifies only the place God chooses (v.2) and the content of the declaration (v.5).
- Distractor 1 is wrong (wrong_detail): It is true that the offering is to the LORD (v.10), but it is WRONG IN DETAIL regarding the location (a local altar instead of the place God chooses) and the content of the declaration (a general thanksgiving from v.10 instead of the historical salvation testimony from vv.5-9).
- Distractor 2 is wrong (nearby_passage): The detail 'the priest' appears in vv.3-4 regarding handing over the basket, but it is WRONG because the destination is the place God chooses (v.2), not the priest's house; and the declaration is wrong (the covenant with Abraham is not the content in this passage).
- Distractor 3 is wrong (true_but_off): The phrase 'the land that You have given' reflects the idea in v.10, but it is OUT OF SCOPE because the location 'the entrance of your tent' is incorrect (it must be the place God chooses), and the declaration is overly simple, lacking the mandatory historical salvation testimony (vv.5-9).
options: Bring it to the altar at your local place — recite 'Give to the LORD your God because He has given this land...' (a general thanksgiving for the land)
Bring it to the house of the priest who is serving — recite 'My father Abraham went from Ur to... was promised many descendants...' (a testimony about the covenant with the patriarch)
Bring it to the entrance of your tent — recite 'Here, I bring the firstfruits from the land that You have given me' (a simple declaration when offering)
Bring to PLACE God CHOSE — recite 'My father was a wandering ARAMEAN... led out of Egypt...' (summary creed of Israel's redemption)

content: According to Deuteronomy 4:24, what is the LORD your God? + GOD of what?
explanation: Deuteronomy 4:24 states: 'For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.' The correct answer quotes the two key phrases that describe the nature of the LORD in the context of a warning against idolatry. Distractor 1 ('LOVING') is incorrect because it replaces the characteristic 'jealous' with an attribute that is true but not the wording of this verse, thereby losing the main point about absolute holiness and judgment. Distractor 2 ('ROCK OF STABILITY') is incorrect because it takes a common image from other passages (such as Deuteronomy 32:4, 31) to describe God, but it is not the simile used in verse 4:24. Distractor 3 ('WICKED God') is incorrect because it is a common misunderstanding and completely contrary to the nature of God in Scripture; this is an inaccurate and absurd description.
options: A CONSUMING FIRE — a JEALOUS God
A CONSUMING FIRE — a LOVING God
A ROCK OF STABILITY — a JEALOUS God
A FAITHFUL ONE — a WICKED God

content: According to Deuteronomy 7:25-26, what must Israel do with Canaanite IDOLS? May they take the silver + gold?
explanation: Deuteronomy 7:25-26 teaches: 'The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God. And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.' (ESV). THE CORRECT ANSWER is correct because it fully states the commands: must burn, do not covet the gold and silver, do not bring into your house, and must utterly abhor. DISTRACTOR 1 (close) is wrong on a key detail: instead of 'utterly abhor' it says 'set aside separately,' contradicting the command to consider it devoted to destruction. DISTRACTOR 2 is wrong because it confuses the command with the command to smash carved images elsewhere (e.g., Deuteronomy 12:3), and permits taking the gold and silver, contrary to the prohibition 'do not covet.' DISTRACTOR 3 is based on the common misunderstanding that defiled items can be purified, but Scripture here teaches absolute avoidance and abhorrence, with no 'purification' exception.
options: MUST BURN — do not COVET the silver + gold covering them — do not BRING them into your house (lest you BE SWALLOWED by them) — must SET ASIDE separately
MUST SMASH — MAY take the silver + gold covering them — do not BRING them into your house (lest you BE SWALLOWED by them) — must UTTERLY ABHOR
MUST BURN — do NOT covet silver + gold on them — do NOT bring into house (lest you BE SNARED) — must UTTERLY DETEST
MUST BURY — do not COVET the silver + gold covering them — but MAY bring them into your house (if purified) — must UTTERLY ABHOR

content: According to Deuteronomy 13:6-11, IF a CLOSE one (brother + child + wife + dear friend) SECRETLY ENTICES to other gods — what?
explanation: The correct answer faithfully reflects Deuteronomy 13:6-11, summarizing the command: do not yield, do not listen, show no pity or compassion, and you must put the enticer to death. You must be the first (your hand shall be first) to lay hands on them to put them to death, then all the people shall stone them. The reason is because they have tried to turn you away from the LORD your God. Distractor 1 (close but incorrect) omits the detail 'all the people shall stone them,' an important part of the execution process stated in verses 9-10. Distractor 2 uses 'stone them to death' from other execution laws (e.g., Deuteronomy 21:21), while this passage simply records 'stone them' (v.10) and emphasizes the personal role of the accuser in initiating the killing. Distractor 3 reflects a common misunderstanding of the general judicial process, but this passage specifically emphasizes the personal duty to report and take active part in the execution, not merely reporting to the authorities.
options: Do not yield to them, do not listen to them, show no pity or compassion; you must put them to death—your hand shall be first against them to put them to death—because they have tried to turn you away from the LORD your God.
Do not yield to them, do not listen to them, show no pity or compassion; you must put them to death—all the people shall stone them—because they have tried to turn you away from the LORD your God.
Secretly report them to the priest and the judge so they may judge, then all the people shall stone that person—because they have tried to turn you away from the LORD your God.
Do NOT consent + DO NOT listen + DO NOT pity + DO NOT spare; you must KILL them — your HAND first, then ALL the people stone; for they tried to LURE you from the LORD

content: According to Deuteronomy 15:7-11, regarding the POOR among Israel, what must the wealthy DO?
explanation:
In Deuteronomy 15:7-11, the question asks about what the Israelites MUST DO regarding the poor. The correct answer is based on verses 7-8, 9, and 11, summarizing the commands: do not harden your heart or close your hand; you must open your hand and lend sufficiently according to the need; do not refuse because the year of release is near, for the poor will cry out and you will be guilty.

- DISTRACTOR 1 (Incorrect detail): It is incorrect in the phrase 'FINED.' The Scripture only warns they will 'be guilty' before the LORD (v.9) and does not prescribe a specific monetary penalty in this passage.

- DISTRACTOR 2 (Incorrect scope): It is incorrect in 'give outright.' This Scripture passage (v.8) speaks of 'lending' sufficiently, not 'giving' outright. The scope of the command is altered to a different form of assistance not specified in the question.

- DISTRACTOR 3 (Common misunderstanding): The actions 'praise and intercede,' while good, are not what this law in Deuteronomy 15:7-11 requires. This is a common misunderstanding of applying general ethical principles (like encouragement, prayer) to a specific command about material action.
options: Do not harden your heart or close your hand—you must open your hand wide and lend enough to meet the person's need; do not think 'the seventh year is near' (the year of release) and refuse to give—for the poor will cry out to the LORD, and you will be guilty AND FINED.
DO NOT HARDEN HEART + DO NOT SHUT HAND — OPEN your hand + lend ENOUGH for what they NEED; do NOT think 'year 7 is NEAR' (debt cancellation) and refuse — the POOR will CRY to LORD, you'll BE GUILTY
Do not harden your heart—you must give outright; do not think 'the seventh year is near' and refuse to give—for the poor will cry out to the LORD, and you will be guilty.
You must praise the poor and intercede for them; do not think 'the seventh year is near' and refuse to give—for the poor will cry out to the LORD, and you will be guilty.

content: According to Deuteronomy 17:8-13, DIFFICULT JUDGMENTS (disputes, manslaughter, lawsuits) — bring where? Final RULING by whom?
explanation:
The correct answer is based on Deuteronomy 17:8-13. Difficult cases for judgment must be brought to the place God chooses (v.8). There, the Levitical priests and the judge in office shall inquire and declare the verdict (v.9-11). The person who acts presumptuously and does not obey that verdict shall die (v.12-13).

Distractor 1 (go to the local altar — the elders) is wrong because it mistakenly applies the scope of ordinary judgment (as in Deuteronomy 16:18-20, 21:1-9) to these special 'cases too difficult for you,' which must be taken to the central authority.

Distractor 2 (only the judges) is a 'close but incorrect' answer because it has the right location but is wrong about the ruling authority, omitting the crucial role of the Levitical priests clearly stated in verses 9 and 12.

Distractor 3 (they consult; the people decide for themselves) is wrong because it misunderstands the nature of the verdict. The Scripture (v.10-11) emphasizes that the people must act according to what they instruct, not decide for themselves; this is a command, not a consultation.
options: Go to the local ALTAR — the elders in the city — they JUDGE disputes; whoever does NOT obey WILL be punished
Go to the PLACE GOD CHOOSES — only the JUDGES — they ISSUE a verdict; whoever does NOT obey WILL be reprimanded
To the PLACE God CHOSE — Levitical PRIESTS + JUDGE — they DECIDE the verdict; disobedience = DEATH
Go to the PLACE GOD CHOOSES — the Levitical PRIESTS + the JUDGES — they CONSULT; the people DECIDE FOR THEMSELVES according to their own will

content: According to Deuteronomy 22:6-7, if you find a NEST with mother bird sitting — what may you do + NOT do?
explanation:
Deuteronomy 22:6-7 teaches: 'If you come across a bird's nest beside the road, either in a tree or on the ground, and the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs, do not take the mother with the young. You may take the young, but be sure to let the mother go, so that it may go well with you and you may have a long life.' (NIV).

- CORRECT ANSWER: Matches Scripture — you are permitted to take the young/eggs, you are not permitted to take the mother bird, and you must let the mother bird go to receive blessing and long life.

- DISTRACTOR 1 (close but incorrect in detail): Incorrect because it reverses the object — Scripture forbids taking the mother bird, not the young birds. The command to 'let go' also applies to the mother bird, not the young birds.
- DISTRACTOR 2 (incorrect in scope): Incorrect because it expands the permission — Scripture only permits taking the young/eggs; it does not permit taking the mother bird. 'Destroying the nest' is not mentioned as a specifically forbidden action in this question's context.
- DISTRACTOR 3 (common misunderstanding): Incorrect because it adds a non-existent ritual — Scripture states the purpose is to 'be blessed and live long' through the obedient act of letting the mother bird go; it never requires offering the mother bird as a sacrifice.
options: May take the YOUNG + eggs — but NOT take the MOTHER + young — must LET the MOTHER GO for BLESSING + long life
You may take the mother bird or the eggs — but DO NOT take the young birds that are with their mother — you must let the young birds go so that you may be blessed and live long
You may take the mother bird and the young birds — but DO NOT destroy the nest — you must leave the nest intact so that you may be blessed and live long
You may take the young birds or the eggs — but DO NOT take the mother bird that is with her young/eggs — you must offer the mother bird to the LORD so that you may be blessed

content: According to Deuteronomy 25:5-10, the LEVIRATE LAW — if a husband DIES without sons — the brother-in-law must do what?
explanation: The correct answer is based on Deuteronomy 25:5-6: 'If brethren dwell together, and one of them die... her husband's brother shall... take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her. And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.' (KJV). This clearly states the duty to marry the widow and that the firstborn son must bear the dead brother's name. The distractors are incorrect as follows: (1) Detail error: this option is correct in structure and the consequence of refusal, but incorrect in stating 'second child' instead of 'firstborn' (verse 6). (2) Scope error: this describes a different regulation concerning divorce or inheritance (see Deuteronomy 24:1-4, 21:15-17), not the levirate marriage law. (3) Common misunderstanding: the primary purpose is for the dead brother's name and lineage not to be blotted out, not merely for general continuation of the line; and the child must bear the dead brother's name, not the living brother's own name (verse 6).
options: MUST MARRY HIS BROTHER'S WIFE (establish a family) — the SECOND CHILD bears the DEAD BROTHER'S NAME — so the FAMILY NAME is NOT LOST; if REFUSED: the WIFE removes his SANDAL, spits in his FACE, and his FAMILY is called 'THE HOUSE OF HIM THAT HATH HIS SHOE LOOSED'

MUST LET HIS BROTHER'S WIFE RETURN TO HER PARENTS' HOUSE — the INHERITANCE is DIVIDED — to PROTECT the property; if REFUSED: the WIFE removes his SANDAL, spits in his FACE, and his FAMILY is called 'THE HOUSE OF HIM THAT HATH HIS SHOE LOOSED'

content: According to Deuteronomy 33:26-29, MOSES blessed Israel — NO one (NATION) is LIKE whom?
explanation:
The question asks about Moses's blessing in Deuteronomy 33:26-29, specifically emphasizing the uniqueness of Israel. The correct answer is from Deuteronomy 33:26, 29: 'There is no one like the God of Jeshurun... Blessed are you, O Israel!...' and 'the LORD is your shield and helper, and the sword of your glory.' The phrase 'sword of your glory' is accurate.

Distractor 1 (close but incorrect detail): Replaces 'sword of your glory' with 'sword of your triumph.' While the idea is similar, the original text uses 'glory.'

Distractor 2 (incorrect scope): Replaces 'Israel' with 'O tribes.' Although Israel comprises the tribes, the blessing in this verse directly addresses 'Israel' as a whole, not individually as 'the tribes.'

Distractor 3 (common misunderstanding): Replaces 'Israel' with 'the LORD.' This is a common misreading, as the preceding verse says 'There is no one like the God...', but the question and answer are about which 'people' is like no other, i.e., Israel, not the LORD.
options: There is no one like Israel—a people saved by God—the LORD is your shield and helper, and the sword of your triumph; blessed are you, Israel!
NO NATION like ISRAEL — saved by God — the LORD is your SHIELD + the SWORD of GLORY; HAPPY are you, ISRAEL!
There is no one like Israel—a people saved by God—the LORD is your shield and helper, and the sword of glory; blessed are you, O tribes!
There is no one like the LORD—a people saved by God—the LORD is your shield and helper, and the sword of glory; blessed are you, Israel!

content: According to Deuteronomy 1:2, how many days did the journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (by the way of Mount Seir) take?
options: Seven days
Forty days
Eleven days
Three days
explanation: ESV Deut 1:2: 'It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea.' (1) 'Forty days' confuses the number with the forty years of wandering in the wilderness (wrong_detail). (2) 'Seven days' is a familiar biblical number but is not the number of days referenced here (wrong_detail). (3) 'Three days' recalls a different three-day journey elsewhere in the Pentateuch, wrong scope (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 1:13-15, on what criteria did Moses base his selection of leaders for the people?
options: Strong, courageous, and skilled in warfare
Wise, understanding, and reputable
Old in age, wealthy, and with many descendants
Of priestly lineage and knowledgeable in offering sacrifices
explanation: ESV Deut 1:13-15: Moses told the people to choose 'wise, understanding, and experienced men' from their tribes, and he appointed them as heads over the people. (1) 'Strong, courageous, and skilled in warfare' sounds plausible for leaders but is not the criteria the text specifies (wrong_detail). (2) 'Old in age, wealthy, and with many descendants' reflects common cultural notions of honor but does not match the stated criteria (common_misconception). (3) 'Of priestly lineage and knowledgeable in offering sacrifices' confuses the role of the Levitical priests with the role of civil leaders and judges (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 1:15, what ranks of leaders did Moses appoint to govern the people?
options: Leaders of thousands, five hundreds, hundreds, and fifties
Leaders of ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, and tens
Leaders of hundreds, fifties, twenties, and tens
Leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens
explanation: ESV Deut 1:15: Moses set them 'as commanders over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers for your tribes.' (1) 'Ten thousands' does not appear among the listed ranks (wrong_detail). (2) The set 'hundreds, fifties, twenties, tens' is wrong because it omits the rank of thousands and adds a rank of twenties (wrong_detail). (3) The set 'thousands, five hundreds, hundreds, fifties' inserts the rank of five hundreds, which is not in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 1:23, how many men did Moses choose to spy out the land, and how were they allocated?
options: Twelve men, one from each tribe
Ten men, chosen from among the elders
Seventy men, the elders of the people
Two men, sent secretly to spy
explanation: ESV Deut 1:23: 'And I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe.' (1) 'Ten men, the elders' is wrong in both the number and the method of selection (wrong_detail). (2) 'Seventy elders' is confused with the seventy elders appointed to assist Moses at a different point in the narrative (near_passage). (3) 'Two men sent secretly' refers to the spying of Jericho in the time of Joshua, which is the wrong scope (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 2:4-5, why did the LORD forbid the Israelites from making war against the descendants of Esau at Mount Seir?
options: Because it was time to return to Horeb and not yet time to take the land
Because the Edomites were too numerous and powerful for Israel to defeat
Because Israel was still bound by a peace treaty previously made with Esau
Because He had given Mount Seir to the descendants of Esau as their possession
explanation: ESV Deut 2:5: 'Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.' (1) 'The Edomites were too numerous and powerful' sounds plausible, but the reason the text gives is God's grant of ownership, not the enemy's military strength (true_but_off). (2) 'A peace treaty previously made with Esau' invents a covenant not found in this passage (wrong_detail). (3) 'It was time to return to Horeb' is confused with the earlier command to leave Horeb, which is the wrong scope (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 2:9, why did the LORD forbid Israel from seizing the land of Moab?
options: Because Moab was a blood brother sharing the same father as Israel
Because He had given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession
Because the Moabites had allowed Israel to pass through their land in peace
Because the land of Moab was entirely rugged mountains unfit for cultivation
explanation: ESV Deut 2:9: 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.' (1) 'Blood brother sharing the same father' is wrong: Moab descends from Lot (Abraham's nephew), not from Esau who was Jacob's own brother (wrong_detail, almost-right since there is a family relationship, but the nature of that relationship is wrong). (2) 'Moab allowed them to pass through in peace' contradicts the broader narrative and is not the reason given in the text (true_but_off). (3) 'The land is entirely rugged mountains' fabricates a geographical reason that does not appear in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 2:10-12, what characteristic do the ancient peoples the Emim, the Horites, and the Anakim share as noted in the text?
options: They were large peoples counted as Rephaim who had previously dwelt in the land before being displaced by other peoples
They were all descendants of Lot who settled around the Dead Sea before Israel
They were Amorite kings defeated by Israel east of the Jordan River
They were peoples whom God forbade Israel to touch because they were Esau's possession
explanation: ESV Deut 2:10-12: The Emim 'were a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim... Like the Anakim they are counted as Rephaim'; the Horites formerly lived in Seir but were driven out and replaced by the descendants of Esau. (1) 'Descendants of Lot around the Dead Sea' confuses the Emim with the Moabites/Ammonites who replaced them, not the peoples themselves (wrong_scope, almost-right). (2) 'Amorite kings east of the Jordan' crosses into the account of Sihon and Og in the following chapter (near_passage, almost-right). (3) 'Peoples forbidden to be touched because they were Esau's possession' wrongly applies the reason given specifically for Seir to the entire group (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 2:14, the period from leaving Kadesh-barnea until crossing the Wadi Zered was associated with which event involving the older generation?
options: Seven years, the time the people waited until they reached the bank of the Wadi Zered
A full forty years, corresponding to one year for each day the land was spied out
Thirty-eight years, until the entire generation of warriors had perished from the camp
One generation, until both Moses and Aaron died outside the promised land
explanation: Deut 2:14 (ESV): 'And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp.' (1) 'Forty years, one year for each day of spying' is a real counting principle found in Numbers, but the number stated in this specific passage is thirty-eight years for this particular stretch (true_but_off, almost-right). (2) 'Seven years waiting to reach the bank of the wadi' invents a number not found in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'Until Moses and Aaron both died' is incorrect because the text's milestone is the death of the entire warrior generation, not the two leaders (wrong_scope, almost-right).

content: According to Deuteronomy 2:19, when Israel drew near to the Ammonites, what did the LORD instruct them?
options: Do not enter their land, because the Ammonites worshiped the detestable god Molech
Take possession of the land of Ammon, for it is the portion the LORD promised to Israel
Buy food and water from them with silver and then pass through
Do not harass or provoke them to war, for that land has been given to the descendants of Lot
explanation: Deut 2:19 (ESV): 'And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.' (1) 'Take possession because it is the LORD's promised portion' directly contradicts the command (wrong_detail). (2) 'Buy food and water with silver and pass through' is the instruction given for passing through Esau's territory in Deut 2:6, not for Ammon (near_passage, almost-right). (3) 'Because they worship Molech' is a historically accurate detail found elsewhere but is not the reason stated in this passage (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 2:24, after crossing the Wadi Arnon, whom did the LORD tell Israel to begin fighting?
options: Arad, the Canaanite king of the Negeb
Og, king of Bashan, one of the Rephaim
Balak, king of Moab
Sihon, king of Heshbon, the Amorite
explanation: Deut 2:24 (ESV): 'Rise up, set out on your journey and cross the Wadi Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land.' (1) 'Og, king of Bashan' is the king defeated later in chapter 3, not at the Wadi Arnon (near_passage). (2) 'Balak, king of Moab' is confused with the figure who hired Balaam; moreover, Moab was commanded not to be attacked (wrong_scope). (3) 'Arad, the Canaanite king of the Negeb' is a king from a different part of the journey and the wrong region (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 3, at which city did the Israelites engage and defeat Og king of Bashan?
options: Heshbon
Edrei
Jabbok
Salecah
explanation: Deut 3:1 (ESV): 'Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.' The battle with Og therefore took place at Edrei. (1) 'Heshbon' is the capital of Sihon the Amorite king from chapter 2, not Og (near_passage). (2) 'Jabbok' is the boundary stream marking the edge of Sihon's territory, not a battle city (wrong_detail). (3) 'Salecah' is a city within Bashan that was captured afterward, not the site of the battle (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 3, how many cities did the Israelites capture in the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan?
options: Thirty cities
Twelve cities
Sixty cities
One hundred cities
explanation: Deut 3:4 (ESV): 'And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.' The correct number is therefore sixty. (1) 'Thirty cities' is an incorrect number (wrong_detail). (2) 'Twelve cities' does not match the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'One hundred cities' overstates the number (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 3, what name did the Sidonians give to Mount Hermon?
options: Pisgah
Sirion
Argob
Senir
explanation: Deuteronomy 3:9 (ESV): 'the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir.' So the name used by the Sidonians is Sirion. (1) 'Pisgah' is the mountain peak from which Moses viewed the promised land and has no connection to Hermon (wrong_scope). (2) 'Argob' is a region of Bashan, not a name for this mountain (wrong_scope). (3) 'Senir' is the name the Amorites used, not the Sidonians (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 4, what did God write on the two stone tablets and command the Israelites to observe?
options: The Ten Commandments
The list of cities of refuge
The laws concerning offerings
The Song of Moses
explanation: Deuteronomy 4:13 (ESV): 'And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone.' So what was inscribed on the two stone tablets is the Ten Commandments. (1) 'The Song of Moses' appears in chapter 32 and was not written on stone tablets (near_passage). (2) 'The list of cities of refuge' appears later in chapter 4 but is not the content of the two stone tablets (true_but_off). (3) 'The laws concerning offerings' belong to other legal portions of Scripture, not the two stone tablets (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 3, what did Moses require of the fighting men from the two and a half tribes who had received their land east of the Jordan, before they were permitted to return to their inheritance?
options: To take up arms and cross the river, marching in the vanguard before their brothers until they too had found rest in the land
To remain and guard the land of Bashan until the conquest on the western side of the river was complete
To give a tenth of the plunder taken from Sihon and Og to the priests
To immediately build fortified cities to protect their wives and children from the remaining Rephaim
explanation: Deuteronomy 3:18–20 (ESV): Moses commanded 'all the men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers' until the LORD gave rest to their brothers across the river, after which they could return to their inheritance. So the condition was to cross over armed as the vanguard. (1) 'Remaining to guard the land of Bashan' is the opposite of the command to march ahead as the vanguard (wrong_detail). (2) 'Giving a tenth of the plunder' is not mentioned anywhere in this passage (wrong_scope). (3) 'Immediately building fortified cities' confuses the prior provision of leaving wives and children in already-established towns with the condition for returning — it is not the command given here (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 4, what reason did Moses give for warning the Israelites not to make carved images in any form?
options: The surrounding nations that worshiped idols had been destroyed by God from the face of the earth
On the day God spoke from the midst of the fire at Horeb, they saw no form whatsoever
Carved images would decay and could not accompany them into the promised land
Only priests were permitted to make sacred objects for use in worship
explanation: Deuteronomy 4:15–16 (ESV): 'Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure.' So the core reason is that they saw no form. (1) 'Idol-worshiping nations being destroyed' is a valid general argument but is not the reason Moses gives at this point (true_but_off). (2) 'Carved images will decay' does not appear in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'Only priests may make sacred objects' shifts to priestly law and misses the point entirely (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 3, after the LORD refused to let Moses enter the promised land, what did He tell Moses to do instead?
options: Return to Horeb and offer a sin offering so that God might change His mind
Choose twelve men to spy out the land from across the Jordan River
Go up to the top of Pisgah, view the land with his own eyes, then commission and encourage Joshua
Immediately divide the promised land among the remaining nine and a half tribes by casting lots
explanation: Deuteronomy 3:27–28 (ESV): 'Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes... And commission Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him.' So God told Moses to view the land from Pisgah and to entrust the task to Joshua. (1) 'Returning to Horeb to offer a sacrifice so God would change His mind' contradicts the text, which states that God firmly refused to listen to Moses' plea (wrong_detail). (2) 'Choosing twelve spies' confuses this with the earlier event at Kadesh (near_passage). (3) 'Immediately dividing the land among the nine and a half tribes by lot' was Joshua's task later — it was not the command given to Moses at this moment (true_but_off).
tags: Moses Forbidden from Entering the Land

content: According to Deuteronomy 4, what image does Moses use to describe Egypt, from which the LORD brought Israel out?
options: A lion's pit
An iron furnace
A dry wilderness
A bronze prison
explanation: Deuteronomy 4:20 (ESV): 'But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance.' The correct image is an iron furnace. (1) 'A lion's pit' is a metaphor for trouble found in other books, not a description of Egypt in this passage (wrong_scope). (2) 'A dry wilderness' describes the journey after leaving Egypt, not Egypt itself (near_passage). (3) 'A bronze prison' sounds plausible but uses the wrong material and image from the text (wrong_detail).

content: Deuteronomy 4 records that Moses set apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan River. Which of the following correctly matches each city to its tribe?
options: Bezer for Reuben, Ramoth for Gad, Golan for Manasseh
Ramoth for Reuben, Golan for Gad, Bezer for Manasseh
Bezer for Gad, Ramoth for Manasseh, Golan for Reuben
Golan for Reuben, Bezer for Manasseh, Ramoth for Gad
explanation: Deuteronomy 4:43 (ESV): 'Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland belonging to the Reubenites; Ramoth in Gilead belonging to the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan belonging to the Manassites.' The correct pairings are Bezer–Reuben, Ramoth–Gad, Golan–Manasseh. (1) This option swaps Bezer to Gad and Golan to Reuben (wrong_detail). (2) This option assigns Ramoth to Reuben and Bezer to Manasseh, getting all positions wrong (wrong_detail). (3) This option scrambles all three pairings, placing Golan with Reuben (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 3, how was the land of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og, divided?
options: All of Gilead to Gad, and all of Bashan divided equally between Reuben and Manasseh
Both Gilead and Bashan belonged entirely to the half-tribe of Manasseh because they had the largest army
Half the hill country of Gilead to Reuben and Gad, and the rest of Gilead together with all of Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh
Reuben received all of Bashan, Gad received all of Gilead, and Manasseh received the region of Argob
explanation: Deuteronomy 3:12-13 (ESV): 'I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites... half the hill country of Gilead with its cities. The rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og... I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh.' So Reuben and Gad received half the hill country of Gilead, while the half-tribe of Manasseh received the remaining part of Gilead and all of Bashan. (1) 'All of Gilead to Gad, and Bashan divided equally between Reuben and Manasseh' gives an incorrect division (wrong_detail). (2) 'Both Gilead and Bashan belonged entirely to Manasseh' omits the portions given to Reuben and Gad (wrong_scope). (3) 'Reuben received all of Bashan, Gad received all of Gilead' reverses the land allocations from the text (wrong_detail).
tags: Land Division of the Two-and-a-Half Tribes

content: According to Deuteronomy 5:15, what must the people of Israel remember as the reason for keeping the Sabbath?
options: They were once slaves in Egypt and God delivered them
God created the heavens and the earth in six days
They wandered forty years in the wilderness
Their ancestors made a covenant at Mount Moriah
explanation: Deuteronomy 5:15 (ESV): 'You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.' The reason given in Deuteronomy is deliverance from slavery in Egypt. (1) 'God created the heavens and the earth in six days' is the reason given in Exodus 20:11, NOT in Deuteronomy 5 (near_passage, confused with Exod 20). (2) 'They wandered forty years in the wilderness' is a true detail found in the book but is not the stated reason for keeping the Sabbath here (true_but_off). (3) 'Their ancestors made a covenant at Mount Moriah' is incorrect; Moriah is associated with the offering of Isaac, not the Sabbath (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 6:8, where on the body must the people bind God's words as a sign?
options: On the forehead and around the neck
On the chest and both shoulders
On the lips and the palms of the hands
On the hand and between the eyes
explanation: Deuteronomy 6:8 (ESV): 'You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.' The correct answer is 'on the hand and between the eyes.' (1) 'On the forehead and around the neck' is incorrect; the text says 'between your eyes,' not around the neck (wrong_detail). (2) 'On the chest and both shoulders' is where the priestly ephod was fastened (Exod 28), not what is commanded here (near_passage). (3) 'On the lips and the palms of the hands' does not appear in this verse (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 6:9, where were the people to write the words of the LORD?
options: On stone tablets placed at the altar
On a scroll entrusted to the priests
On a stone pillar erected in the middle of the city
On the doorposts of your house and on your gates
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 6:9 reads: 'You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.' The correct answer is 'on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.' (1) 'Stone tablets placed at the altar' conflates the tablets of testimony or altar references in other passages, not this verse (near_passage). (2) 'A scroll entrusted to the priests' suggests the king's act of copying the law (Deut 17:18), not this passage (near_passage). (3) 'A stone pillar erected in the middle of the city' is a wrong detail — the text speaks of the doorposts and gates of each individual household (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 5:16, what promise accompanies the commandment to honor your father and mother?
options: That you may overcome all your enemies
That your descendants may be as numerous as the stars in the sky
That your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land
That the LORD may send timely rain on your fields
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 5:16 reads: 'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.' The promise is to live long and fare well in the land. (1) 'Descendants as numerous as the stars' is the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15), not attached to this commandment (near_passage). (2) 'Overcome all your enemies' is not the content of the promise in the commandment to honor parents (wrong_detail). (3) 'Timely rain on your fields' is a real blessing found in Deuteronomy 11 but is not attached to this commandment (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 5:24-27, why did the Israelites ask Moses to stand as a mediator and hear the words of the LORD on their behalf?
options: Because they could not understand the voice speaking from the mountain
Because they feared they would die from the great fire if they continued to hear the voice of the LORD
Because they were in a hurry to advance and take possession of Canaan
Because the elders had been chosen to represent the whole people
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 5:25 records the people saying: 'Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die.' The reason was the fear of dying from the fire when hearing the LORD's voice directly. (1) 'Could not understand the voice speaking' is wrong: the people heard and understood — the issue was fear of death, not incomprehension (wrong_detail). (2) 'In a hurry to advance and take Canaan' is irrelevant; that time had not yet come (true_but_off / wrong context). (3) 'The elders had been chosen to represent the people' confuses this with the appointment of the seventy elders (Numbers 11), which is not the reason given here (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 6:7, how were parents to teach the words of the LORD to their children?
options: Diligently, talking about them when sitting at home, walking by the way, lying down, and rising
Only solemnly on the Sabbath at the place of assembly
By entrusting the priests and Levites to teach in their place at the temple
Only once a year during the major appointed feasts
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 6:7 reads: 'You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.' The teaching must be continuous, woven into every aspect of daily life. (1) 'Only on the Sabbath at the place of assembly' wrongly limits the scope, contrary to the command's expectation of teaching at all times and in all places (wrong_scope). (2) 'Entrusting the priests and Levites to teach in their place' shifts responsibility to the wrong party — the text addresses parents directly (wrong_scope). (3) 'Once a year during the appointed feasts' misrepresents the frequency; the command requires continual, daily teaching (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 6:10-12, what danger did Moses warn the people about when they entered a land full of fine houses, cisterns, and vineyards they had not built?
options: They would forget the LORD who brought them out of the house of slavery
They would return to being slaves to the Canaanite peoples
They would become proud and despise the poor in the land
They would quarrel over inheritances among the tribes
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 6:12 reads: 'then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.' The danger Moses warned about was forgetting God once the people were well-fed and settled in the land. (1) 'Quarreling over inheritances among the tribes' is not the content of this warning (wrong_detail). (2) 'Returning to being slaves to the Canaanite peoples' confuses the reference to the 'house of slavery' in Egypt in the verse and misidentifies the party (wrong_detail). (3) 'Becoming proud and despising the poor' is a real warning found elsewhere in Scripture but is not the focus of this passage (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 6:20–23, when children ask about the meaning of the laws, what must parents give as the foundational answer?
options: Describe the majesty of Mount Sinai when the law was given
Recount how the LORD delivered them from the hand of Pharaoh in Egypt
List the full Ten Commandments in exact order
Tell the story of the patriarch Abraham being called to leave Ur
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 6:21 records the answer parents must give: 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.' The foundational answer is to recount the deliverance from Egypt. (1) 'Describing the majesty of Mount Sinai' is a real detail in the book but is not the answer taught here (true_but_off). (2) 'Listing the full Ten Commandments in order' is not the content of this reply (wrong_detail). (3) 'Telling the story of Abraham leaving Ur' crosses over into Genesis and is not the designated answer (near_passage).

content: In what core way does the reason for keeping the Sabbath in the Ten Commandments of Deuteronomy 5 differ from the version in Exodus 20?
options: Deuteronomy moves the rest day to the first day, while Exodus 20 keeps the seventh day
Deuteronomy forbids all work, while Exodus 20 only prohibits trading
Deuteronomy emphasizes deliverance from slavery, while Exodus 20 emphasizes the work of creation
Deuteronomy only requires the head of household to rest, while Exodus 20 requires servants to rest as well
explanation: Deuteronomy 5:15 gives the reason: 'You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day' — linking the Sabbath to deliverance from slavery. Exodus 20:11, by contrast, gives the reason: 'For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy' — linking it to the work of creation. (1) 'Forbids all work vs. only prohibits trading' is wrong; both versions prohibit work in general (wrong_detail). (2) 'Moves to the first day' is wrong; both versions keep the seventh day (common_misconception). (3) 'Only the head of household rests vs. servants must also rest' is wrong; both versions require servants and animals to rest — Deuteronomy 5:14 makes this especially explicit (wrong_detail).

content: In the Ten Commandments of Deuteronomy 5, which commandment is accompanied by an explicit promise of reward?
options: The commandment against murder
The commandment to remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy
The commandment against coveting your neighbor's possessions
The commandment to honor your father and mother
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 5:16 is the only commandment in this list accompanied by a promise: 'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.' (1) 'Do not murder' (5:17) is stated plainly, with no accompanying promise (wrong_detail). (2) 'Remember the Sabbath' (5:12–15) includes a reason (slavery in Egypt) rather than a promise of reward to the one who keeps it — easy to confuse because of its lengthy explanation, but that is a reason, not a promise (true_but_off). (3) 'Do not covet your neighbor's possessions' (5:21) also carries no promise (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 7:16, after God delivers the nations into Israel's hand, what attitude must they have toward the gods of those nations?
options: Hand those gods over to the Levites to be stored in the sanctuary
Place those gods in the temple as a witness to their victory
Offer sacrifices to those gods once a year to maintain peaceful relations
Not serve those gods, for they would be a snare to them
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 7:16 states: '...your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.' The correct answer is therefore 'Do not serve those gods, for they would be a snare.' (1) 'Place in the temple as a witness' completely reverses the command — the gods were to be utterly destroyed, not put on display (wrong_detail). (2) 'Offer sacrifices once a year' is absolutely forbidden — a misconception about religious accommodation (common_misconception). (3) 'Hand over to the Levites to store in the sanctuary' confuses the role of guarding holy objects with the wrong subject — foreign gods were to be destroyed, not preserved (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 8:4, what happened — or rather, did NOT happen — to the people of Israel during their 40 years in the wilderness?
options: Their food supply ran out and they went hungry for many days
Their weapons rusted so they could not fight
Their clothing did not wear out and their feet did not swell
Their tents were torn apart one by one by the desert winds
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 8:4 records: 'Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years.' This is a sign of God's supernatural care. (1) 'Food ran out and they went hungry' contradicts the LORD's regular provision of manna (wrong_detail). (2) 'Weapons rusted' is a detail not found in the text — a false inference (wrong_detail). (3) 'Tents torn apart by desert winds' contradicts the theme of preservation in this verse (true_but_off — the harshness of the wilderness is real, but the verse speaks of God's preservation).

content: According to Deuteronomy 7:20, what did God say He would send to drive out those who remain and hide themselves from Israel?
options: A great earthquake to swallow up the cities
Fire from heaven to consume their hiding places
Hornets among them
Hailstones to destroy their fields
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 7:20 reads: 'Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed.' So the correct answer is 'hornets.' (1) 'Earthquake' is not mentioned here — it assigns a wrong instrument of judgment (wrong_detail). (2) 'Fire from heaven' evokes Sodom rather than this passage (near_passage). (3) 'Hailstones' evoke the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9) rather than the instrument for driving out the Canaanites (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 8:5, what image did Moses use to describe how God disciplines the people of Israel?
options: As a shepherd disciplines his flock
As a master trains his servant
As a king judges his subjects
As a father disciplines his son
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 8:5 reads: 'Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.' The image is a father with his son. (1) 'A shepherd with his flock' is a common biblical metaphor but not the image used here (true_but_off). (2) 'A king with his subjects' captures the covenant relationship correctly but misses the specific metaphor of the verse (true_but_off). (3) 'A master with his servant' reflects the earlier imagery of Egyptian slavery rather than a father-son relationship (wrong_detail).

content: Deuteronomy 7:3-4 forbids Israel from intermarrying with the Canaanite peoples. According to the text, what is the core reason for this prohibition?
options: Because those peoples would turn the children of Israel away from the LORD to serve other gods
Because those peoples are of a cursed lineage whose bloodlines must not be mixed
Because marriage to foreigners causes ritual impurity and requires a sin offering
Because those peoples are poor and would gradually deplete Israel's inheritance
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 7:4 states the reason plainly: '...for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly.' So the reason is a spiritual danger — being led into worshiping other gods. (1) 'Cursed lineage, mixing bloodlines' is a racial argument — the text is grounded not in bloodline but in faithfulness to the LORD (common_misconception). (2) 'Ritual impurity requiring a sin offering' sounds plausible within purity law but is not the reason stated here (true_but_off). (3) 'Poor peoples depleting the inheritance' is an economic concern entirely off the spiritual focus of the text (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 7:22, God said He would drive out the Canaanite peoples 'little by little' rather than all at once. What reason does the text give for this approach?
options: So that Israel would have time to learn the languages and customs of those peoples
Lest the wild beasts of the field multiply too greatly against Israel
To test whether Israel would remain patient and obedient to the end
Lest neighboring nations see the empty land and come to occupy it first
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 7:22 reads: 'The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you.' The reason is ecological — if the land is emptied too quickly, wild animals would multiply. (1) 'Learn their language and customs' directly contradicts the command to avoid the influence of foreign peoples (wrong_detail). (2) 'Testing patient obedience' is a genuine theme in the book (8:2) but is not the reason given in this verse (near_passage). (3) 'Neighboring nations coming to occupy the land' is a strategic inference not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: In Deuteronomy 8:11-14, Moses warns the people about a particular danger that would come WHEN in their lives?
options: When they were still wandering hungry and thirsty in the wilderness and prone to grumbling
When they were besieged by neighboring peoples and feared and wanted to return to Egypt
When they had eaten and were full, built fine houses, and their herds, silver, and gold had multiplied
When they had just crossed the Jordan River and had not yet had time to build an altar for the LORD
explanation: ESV Deuteronomy 8:12-14 reads: 'lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied, then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God...' The danger comes in times of prosperity, not in hardship. (1) 'Hungry and thirsty in the wilderness' reverses the circumstances — the text warns of fullness and abundance, not scarcity (wrong_detail). (2) 'Besieged and wanting to return to Egypt' is a real temptation found elsewhere in the Pentateuch but is off the mark for this particular warning (true_but_off). (3) 'Just crossed the Jordan, not yet built an altar' misplaces the timing — the danger comes after Israel has settled, built, and grown wealthy (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 8:19, if Israel forgot God and went after other gods to serve and worship them, what consequence did Moses solemnly warn would come upon them?
options: They would be exiled for seventy years and then allowed to return to the land
They would be enslaved by neighboring nations but still retain the land
They would suffer crop failure and famine for seven consecutive years
They would surely perish
explanation: Deuteronomy 8:19 (ESV) states: '...if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish.' The consequence is total destruction. (1) 'Exile for seventy years' is Jeremiah's prophecy concerning Babylon, not this passage (near_passage). (2) 'Crop failure and famine for seven years' is a different type of covenant curse found in Leviticus, not the statement here (near_passage). (3) 'Enslaved but still retaining the land' softens the punishment — the text says 'surely perish,' not that they would keep the land (wrong_detail).

content: Deuteronomy 8:20 uses a comparison to emphasize the fate awaiting Israel if they do not obey the Lord. That fate is likened to what?
options: The same as Sodom and Gomorrah being destroyed by fire
The same as the generation that fell dead in the wilderness for their unbelief
The same as the nations the LORD is destroying before them
The same as Pharaoh and the Egyptian army buried beneath the Red Sea
explanation: Deuteronomy 8:20 (ESV) states: 'Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.' The comparison is 'like those nations' destroyed by the LORD — specifically the Canaanite peoples. This is the bitter irony: if they disobey, Israel will suffer the exact fate of the nations they have just driven out. (1) 'The generation that fell dead in the wilderness' is a real judgment event (Numbers 14) and is therefore very attractive, but it is not the comparison used in this verse (near_passage, almost-right). (2) 'Sodom and Gomorrah' is a classic symbol of judgment used elsewhere, but not the image invoked here (near_passage, almost-right). (3) 'Pharaoh under the Red Sea' reverses the roles — that event was Israel's redemption, not a model for their own destruction (wrong_scope).

content: Deuteronomy 7:1–2 commands the 'utter destruction' of the Canaanite peoples, yet 7:22 says God will drive them out 'little by little' and not 'quickly.' Reading the text carefully, which interpretation best explains this apparent tension?
options: The ultimate goal remains total destruction; 'little by little' addresses only the pace for practical reasons
The command for utter destruction applies only to the kings of those nations; the common people are to be driven out gradually
Verse 7:2 is merely conditional; verse 7:22 actually cancels the destruction command and replaces it with gradual expulsion
Utter destruction applies when Israel wins battles; gradual expulsion applies when they lose
explanation: Deuteronomy 7:22 (ESV) states: 'you may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you,' and 7:24 still affirms 'you shall make their name perish from under heaven.' The ultimate goal (total destruction) is therefore unchanged; 'little by little' adjusts only the PACE for practical reasons — occupying the land too quickly would leave it desolate and allow wild animals to multiply and endanger the people. (1) 'Destroy only the kings, drive out the commoners gradually' is a distinction not found in the text (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) '7:22 cancels the destruction command' misreads the passage — 7:24 shows the command remains fully in force; only the timeline is extended (wrong_detail, almost-right). (3) 'Destroy when victorious, drive out when losing' invents a win-or-lose condition that is not present; the text gives an ecological reason, not a battle-outcome condition (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 9:6, how does Moses describe the people of Israel?
options: A stubborn people
A holy people
A people as numerous as the stars of heaven
A people fewer in number than all peoples
explanation: Deuteronomy 9:6 (ESV): 'Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.' The correct answer is 'A stubborn people.' (1) 'A holy people' is drawn from a description found elsewhere (Deut 7:6) and incorrectly assigned to this verse (true_but_off). (2) 'A people as numerous as the stars of heaven' refers to Israel's great numbers in Deut 10:22, not the character trait being rebuked here (near_passage). (3) 'A people fewer in number than all peoples' draws from the idea in Deut 7:7 that Israel was originally small, which misses the focus of this verse (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 9:9–11, how long was Moses on Mount Horeb when he received the two stone tablets of the covenant, eating no bread and drinking no water?
options: Forty days and forty nights
Seven days and seven nights
Three days and three nights
Six days, until the seventh day
explanation: Deuteronomy 9:9 (ESV): 'When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.' The correct answer is 'Forty days and forty nights.' (1) 'Seven days and seven nights' is simply an incorrect number (wrong_detail). (2) 'Three days and three nights' is also an incorrect number (wrong_detail), pointing to a different cycle found elsewhere in Scripture. (3) 'Six days, until the seventh day' is drawn from the pattern of the cloud covering Mount Sinai in Exodus 24:16, which is a different passage and off-topic here (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 9:16-17, when Moses came down from the mountain and saw that the people had made a cast idol of a calf, what did he do with the two stone tablets?
options: He hid the two stone tablets in a wooden ark
He threw the two stone tablets down and broke them before the eyes of the people
He handed the two stone tablets to Aaron to keep
He carried the two stone tablets back up the mountain to the LORD
explanation: Deuteronomy 9:17 (ESV): 'And I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.' The correct answer is 'He threw the two stone tablets down and broke them before the eyes of the people.' (1) 'Hid them in a wooden ark' borrows the detail of the NEW tablets being placed in the ark in Deut 10:5, misplacing the timeline of the question (near_passage). (2) 'Handed them to Aaron to keep' confuses Aaron's role — he was the one who made the calf idol, not someone who kept the tablets (wrong_scope). (3) 'Carried them back up the mountain to the LORD' is a plausible action but not what the text records (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 9:20, why did Moses also have to intercede for Aaron at that time?
options: Because Aaron had seized the inheritance of the tribe of Levi
Because Aaron had refused to lead the people into the promised land
Because the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him
Because Aaron spoke against Moses in front of the people
explanation: Deuteronomy 9:20 (ESV): 'And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time.' The correct answer is 'Because the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him.' (1) 'Refused to lead the people into the promised land' is not found in the text (wrong_detail). (2) 'Seized the inheritance of the tribe of Levi' reverses the truth — the tribe of Levi has NO inheritance (Deut 10:9), making this off-topic here (true_but_off). (3) 'Spoke against Moses' confuses this event with the incident involving Miriam and Aaron in Numbers 12 (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 10:1-3, after cutting two new stone tablets, what did God command Moses to make in order to hold them?
options: A chest of gold
An ark of wood
An altar of stone
A tent of animal skins
explanation: Deuteronomy 10:1 (ESV): 'Carve out two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood.' The correct answer is 'An ark of wood.' (1) 'A chest of gold' confuses this with the ark of the covenant overlaid with gold described in Exodus 25, applying the wrong material to what is stated here (wrong_detail). (2) 'An altar of stone' draws on the command in Deut 27:5-6 about the stone altar at Mount Ebal, which is off-topic (near_passage). (3) 'A tent of animal skins' confuses this with the coverings of the Tabernacle in Exodus 26 (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 10:9, why does the tribe of Levi have no portion or inheritance like the other tribes?
options: Because they made the golden calf at Horeb
Because the LORD is their inheritance
Because they are the smallest tribe
Because they stayed on the other side of the Jordan River
explanation: Deuteronomy 10:9 (ESV): 'Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.' The correct answer is 'Because the LORD is their inheritance.' (1) 'Made the golden calf' is a misconception — the tribe of Levi actually stood with Moses after the golden calf incident (Exodus 32:26), so this is exactly backwards (common_misconception). (2) 'The smallest tribe' is a fabricated reason not found in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'Stayed on the other side of the Jordan' confuses this with the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh in Numbers 32 (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 10:17-18, which of the following characteristics is stated about God in how He deals with people?
options: He shows no partiality and takes no bribe
He only blesses the wealthy
He only hears the prayers of priests
He changes according to the offerings presented to Him
explanation: Deuteronomy 10:17 (ESV): '...the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe.' The correct answer is 'He shows no partiality and takes no bribe.' The remaining three options all contradict this very verse: (1) 'Only blesses the wealthy' contradicts verse 18, which states that He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (wrong_detail). (2) 'Only hears the prayers of priests' applies a scope far narrower than what the text affirms (wrong_scope). (3) 'Changes according to offerings' is precisely the notion denied by the phrase 'takes no bribe' (common_misconception).

content: Deuteronomy 10:19 commands the people to love the stranger. According to this verse, what reason is given?
options: Because the strangers would help them conquer the land of Canaan
Because the strangers are also descendants of Abraham
Because they themselves were once strangers in the land of Egypt
Because the law requires strangers to pay tithes
explanation: Deuteronomy 10:19 (ESV): 'Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.' The correct answer is 'Because they themselves were once strangers in the land of Egypt.' (1) 'Descendants of Abraham' is wrong in scope — strangers are outsiders, not of Abraham's lineage (wrong_scope). (2) 'Help them conquer the land' is a fabricated pragmatic reason not found in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'Pay tithes' confuses this with the law providing for strangers, orphans, and widows in Deuteronomy 14:29, straying from the question (near_passage).

content: Deuteronomy 11:2-6 reminds the people of the mighty acts they witnessed with their own eyes. Among these, what happened to Dathan and Abiram?
options: They were struck with severe leprosy and driven out of the camp
Fire from heaven consumed them before the entrance of the Tabernacle
The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them along with their households and tents
The sea waters closed over them and buried them along with all their chariots
explanation: Deuteronomy 11:6 (ESV): '...and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel.' The correct answer is 'The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them along with their households and tents.' (1) 'Fire from heaven consumed them' confuses this with the fate of the 250 men who offered incense during the same Korah incident (Numbers 16:35) — a related event but a different manner of death from Dathan and Abiram (near_passage). (2) 'Struck with leprosy and driven out' confuses this with Miriam in Numbers 12 (wrong_detail). (3) 'The sea waters closed over them' confuses this with the Egyptian army at the Red Sea (Exodus 14), another miracle also mentioned in Deuteronomy 11:4 (true_but_off).

content: Deuteronomy 11:10-12 contrasts the land of Canaan with the land of Egypt. According to the text, what is the core difference in how the land is watered?
options: Canaan drinks rainwater from heaven, unlike Egypt which had to be irrigated by foot like a vegetable garden
Canaan is watered by great rivers, while Egypt relies only on rain
Both lands depend on rain from heaven, but Canaan receives more
Canaan requires digging deep wells, while Egypt has natural springs
explanation: Deuteronomy 11:10-11 (ESV): 'For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables. But the land that you are going over to possess... drinks water by the rain from heaven.' The correct answer is 'Canaan drinks rainwater from heaven, unlike Egypt which had to be irrigated by foot like a vegetable garden.' (1) The option saying Canaan relies on rivers while Egypt relies on rain REVERSES what the text actually says (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'Both depend on rain from heaven' erases the very contrast the passage is making (true_but_off). (3) 'Digging deep wells... natural springs' is a fabricated detail not found in the passage (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 12:16, when slaughtering an animal to eat its meat, how must the Israelites handle the blood of the animal?
options: Pour the blood out on the ground like water
Sprinkle the blood on the altar before eating
Keep the blood to use as a sin offering
Mix the blood with salt before eating
explanation: Deuteronomy 12:16 (ESV): 'Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.' The correct answer is 'Pour the blood out on the ground like water.' (1) 'Sprinkle the blood on the altar' confuses this with sacrificial rituals at the sanctuary, which do not apply to meat slaughtered for eating in the towns (near_passage). (2) 'Keep the blood to use as a sin offering' gets the detail wrong: the blood must be poured out, not kept (wrong_detail). (3) 'Mix the blood with salt before eating' directly contradicts the prohibition on consuming blood (common_misconception).

content: According to Deuteronomy 12:32, what are the Israelites commanded to do regarding everything God has commanded them?
options: Be careful to do it; do not add to it or take from it
Write it down to pass it on to future generations
Read it aloud once a year
Do it, but you may adjust it as the times change
explanation: Deuteronomy 12:32 (ESV): 'Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.' The correct answer is 'Be careful to do it; do not add to it or take from it.' (1) 'Write it down to pass it on to future generations' is true within the broader law but is not what this verse emphasizes (true_but_off). (2) 'Read it aloud once a year' confuses this with the command to read the law in Deuteronomy 31, not this verse (near_passage). (3) 'May adjust it as the times change' directly contradicts the command 'you shall not add to it or take from it' (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 14:6, which animals are considered clean and permitted to eat?
options: Animals that have a split hoof but do not chew the cud
Animals that both have a split hoof and chew the cud
Animals that chew the cud but do not have a split hoof
Animals that live both on land and in water
explanation: Deuteronomy 14:6 (ESV): 'Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof split in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.' BOTH signs must be present. The correct answer is 'Animals that both have a split hoof and chew the cud.' (1) 'Animals that have a split hoof but do not chew the cud' satisfies only one condition (e.g., the pig) and is therefore forbidden (wrong_detail). (2) 'Animals that chew the cud but do not have a split hoof' also satisfies only one condition (e.g., the hare) and is therefore forbidden (wrong_detail). (3) 'Animals that live both on land and in water' is not a criterion for distinguishing clean animals in this verse (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 14:9-10, what characteristics must a water creature have in order to be permitted to eat?
options: Hard scales covering its entire body
Fins but no claws
Living in flowing water rather than still water
Fins and scales
explanation: Deuteronomy 14:9-10 (ESV): 'Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat. And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat.' The correct answer is 'Fins and scales.' (1) 'Hard scales covering its entire body' omits the condition of fins and adds a detail not found in the text (wrong_detail). (2) 'Living in flowing water rather than still water' is not a criterion stated anywhere in this law (common_misconception). (3) 'Fins but no claws' lacks the condition of scales and introduces the irrelevant detail of claws (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 12:6-7, where were the Israelites required to bring their burnt offerings, tithes, vow offerings, and freewill offerings?
options: To the house of the nearest Levite in their town
To any high place where their ancestors had worshiped
To the place the LORD would choose to put his name
To the city gate for the elders to distribute
explanation: Deuteronomy 12:6 (ESV): 'And there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings...' — 'there' refers back to 'the place that the LORD your God will choose... to put his name' (v. 5). The correct answer is 'To the place the LORD would choose to put his name.' (1) 'To the house of the nearest Levite' confuses this with the third-year tithe law (14:28-29), which does not apply to these offerings (near_passage). (2) 'To any high place where their ancestors had worshiped' contradicts the command to demolish the high places and centralize worship (wrong_detail). (3) 'To the city gate for the elders to distribute' confuses this with judicial proceedings at the gate, which are unrelated to offerings (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 13:12-16, what fate must befall an Israelite city that has been led astray to worship other gods?
options: It must pay double taxes to the central sanctuary
It must be completely burned and left a ruin forever
Its inhabitants must be expelled from the land and exiled among the nations
Its altars must be torn down and a sin offering presented
explanation: Deuteronomy 13:16 (ESV): 'You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire... It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again.' The correct answer is 'It must be completely burned and left a ruin forever.' (1) 'It must pay double taxes' has no basis in the text and is far too lenient compared to the sentence of destruction (wrong_detail). (2) 'Its inhabitants must be expelled and exiled' confuses this with the later punishment of national exile, not the judgment for an apostate city (near_passage). (3) 'Its altars must be torn down and a sin offering presented' is a lenient resolution nowhere mentioned — the city must be utterly destroyed (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 14:1-2, because they are a holy people belonging to God, what mourning practice were the Israelites forbidden to do for the dead?
options: Bury the dead outside the camp
Wear sackcloth or tear their garments
Fast for more than three days
Cut themselves or shave the front of their heads above their eyes
explanation: Deuteronomy 14:1 (ESV): 'You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead.' These were pagan mourning customs. The correct answer is 'Cut themselves or shave the front of their heads above their eyes.' (1) 'Wear sackcloth or tear their garments' — tearing one's garments was in fact practiced by godly people in the Old Testament (true_but_off). (2) 'Fast for more than three days' — the specific number of three days does not appear in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'Bury the dead outside the camp' confuses this with the purity laws concerning the camp, which are unrelated to mourning rites here (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 14:28-29, the tithe set aside at the end of every third year was designated to provide for whom?
options: For the priests serving at the central sanctuary
For the Levites, the poor, and released prisoners
For soldiers and those who guard the city gates
For the Levites, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow
explanation: Deuteronomy 14:28-29 (ESV): 'At the end of every three years... the Levite... and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled.' The correct answer is 'For the Levites, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.' (1) 'For the priests at the sanctuary' wrongly narrows the recipients — this tithe was for the vulnerable within the towns (wrong_scope). (2) 'For soldiers and those who guard the city gates' is not mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). (3) 'Levites, the poor, and released prisoners' correctly names the Levites but substitutes the other two groups incorrectly (wrong_detail).

content: Deuteronomy 12:30-31 warns the Israelites not to inquire about how the surrounding nations worship their gods in order to imitate them. What core reason does the text give for why such worship is an abomination to the LORD?
options: Because those nations offered precious metals such as gold and silver to their idols
Because they burned their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods
Because they worshiped on the high places instead of in the low places of the land
Because they mixed the worship of the LORD with the worship of other gods
explanation: Deuteronomy 12:31 (ESV): 'for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods.' The text identifies the burning of children in fire as the pinnacle of the abomination. The correct answer is the option stating they 'burned their sons and daughters.' (1) 'Offering precious metals such as gold and silver to idols' misidentifies the core sin — the offense does not lie in the monetary value of the offering (wrong_detail). (2) 'Worshiping on the high places rather than in the low places of the land' confuses the location issue raised in 12:2 with the reason the ritual itself is abominable in nature (near_passage). (3) 'Mixing the worship of the LORD with other gods' is a real danger warned against in v.30 but is not the 'abomination' the text names in v.31 (true_but_off).
