content: Regarding the plunder of an apostate Israelite city (Deuteronomy 13:16-17), what notable rule does the text prescribe that differs from the ordinary treatment of war plunder?
options: A portion of the plunder must be given to the priests, and the rest may be kept
The plunder is to be divided equally among all the tribes of Israel
Nothing under the ban may touch their hands; everything must be burned completely
Gold and silver are kept for the treasury of the LORD, and the rest is burned
explanation: Deuteronomy 13:16-17 (ESV): 'You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire... None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand.' Unlike ordinary plunder, which could be kept, everything here must be utterly destroyed. The correct answer is 'Nothing under the ban may touch their hands; everything must be burned completely.' (1) 'A portion for the priests, and the rest kept' wrongly applies the ordinary rules of plunder from Numbers 31 to this special case (near_passage). (2) 'Divided equally among all the tribes' is likewise how ordinary plunder was distributed and does not apply here (wrong_scope). (3) 'Gold and silver kept for the LORD's treasury' conflates this law with the conquest of Jericho in Joshua 6; in this passage everything must be burned (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 15:12, in what year must an owner release a Hebrew slave who was sold into service?
options: The fifth year
The sixth year
The seventh year
The fiftieth year
explanation: Deuteronomy 15:12 (ESV): 'If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you.' The correct answer is 'The seventh year.' (1) 'The sixth year' gets the detail wrong (wrong_detail): the sixth year is the final year of service; the release takes place in the seventh year. (2) 'The fifth year' states an incorrect number (wrong_detail). (3) 'The fiftieth year' refers to the Year of Jubilee in Leviticus 25, a different release law altogether (true_but_off), not the Hebrew slave law addressed here.

content: According to Deuteronomy 15:13-14, when a Hebrew slave is released in the seventh year, what must the owner do for that person?
options: Let the person go empty-handed, since he has already benefited from six years of provision
Pay the person six years of wages in silver
Provide generously from the flock, the threshing floor, and the winepress
Retain the person's wife and children as compensation for the owner's labor
explanation: Deuteronomy 15:13-14 (ESV): 'And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress.' The correct answer is to provide generously from the flock, the threshing floor, and the winepress. (1) 'Let the person go empty-handed' directly contradicts verse 13, which forbids this (wrong_detail, almost-right because the reasoning sounds plausible but opposes the text). (2) 'Pay six years of wages in silver' is a logical inference based on labor rendered, but the text prescribes giving goods from one's estate, not paying a wage (true_but_off). (3) 'Retain the wife and children' borrows a detail from another scenario in verses 16-17 and Exodus 21:4 (near_passage), which is not what this law prescribes.

content: According to Deuteronomy 15:16-17, if a slave loves his master and wishes to remain as a servant forever, what mark must the master make on him?
options: Pierce his ear with an awl against the door
Lay hands on his head and bless him
Brand a mark on his forehead with a hot iron
Cut off a corner of his garment to keep as a witness
explanation: Deuteronomy 15:17 (ESV): 'then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever.' The correct answer is 'Pierce his ear with an awl against the door.' (1) 'Laying on of hands in blessing' is a genuine biblical ceremony but used in other contexts, not as the mark of a voluntary slave (true_but_off). (2) 'Branding a mark on the forehead with a hot iron' is a slave punishment found in foreign cultures, not in Deuteronomy law (common_misconception). (3) 'Cutting off a corner of the garment to keep as a witness' draws on the motif from David and Saul (near_passage), and is unrelated to this law.

content: According to Deuteronomy 15:19, what must the Israelites do with the firstborn males of their herds and flocks?
options: Sell them for silver to contribute to the temple treasury
Hand them over to the Levites as a substitute for the tithe
Set them apart as holy to the LORD your God
Keep them for breeding to grow the flock larger
explanation: Deuteronomy 15:19 (ESV): 'All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the LORD your God.' The correct answer is 'Set them apart as holy to the LORD.' (1) 'Selling them for silver' contradicts verse 19, which forbids using the firstborn for personal gain — one must not work the firstborn ox or shear the firstborn sheep (wrong_detail). (2) 'Handing them over to the Levites as a substitute for the tithe' confuses this with the tithe-for-Levites system (wrong_scope). (3) 'Keeping them for breeding' is an economic practice but contradicts the command to set them apart as holy (true_but_off).

content: According to Deuteronomy 16:1, in which month must the Israelites observe the Passover for the LORD, and to remember what event?
options: In the month of Abib, because in that month the LORD gave the Ten Commandments at Sinai
In the seventh month, because in that month they entered the Promised Land
In the month of Abib, because in that month the LORD brought them out of Egypt by night
In the third month, because in that month the LORD made a covenant with Abraham
explanation: Deuteronomy 16:1 (ESV): 'Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night.' The correct answer is 'In the month of Abib … brought out of Egypt by night.' (1) 'The seventh month … entered the Promised Land' is wrong on both the month and the reason (wrong_detail). (2) 'The month of Abib … gave the Ten Commandments' has the right month but assigns the wrong event — the giving of the law at Sinai belongs to the Feast of Weeks (true_but_off). (3) 'The third month … covenant with Abraham' is wrong on both the month and the event (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 16:16, three times a year all males must appear before the LORD at which three festivals?
options: The Feast of Passover, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Trumpets
The Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Firstfruits, and the Day of Atonement
The New Moon festival, the Sabbath, and the Feast of Booths
The Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths
explanation: Deuteronomy 16:16 (ESV): 'Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths.' The correct answer is 'The Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths.' (1) 'Passover, Day of Atonement, Feast of Trumpets' lists real feasts from the sacred calendar (Leviticus 23) but not the three pilgrimage feasts specified here (true_but_off). (2) 'New Moon, Sabbath, Feast of Booths' mixes periodic holy days with one correct pilgrimage feast (wrong_scope). (3) 'Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Day of Atonement' gets one right and two wrong (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 16:16-17, when the men appear before the LORD at the three festivals, by what principle must they bring an offering?
options: Each person must bring an equal amount to maintain fairness
No one shall appear empty-handed; each shall give as he is able, according to the blessing the LORD has given him
Only the wealthy are required to bring an offering; the poor are exempt
Each person must bring exactly a tenth of his produce
explanation: Deuteronomy 16:16-17 (ESV): 'None shall appear before the LORD empty-handed. Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.' The correct answer is 'No one shall appear empty-handed; each shall give as he is able, according to the LORD's blessing.' (1) 'Bringing an equal amount' contradicts the principle of giving according to one's ability (wrong_detail). (2) 'Only the wealthy are required to give' contradicts verse 16, which requires all males without exception (wrong_detail). (3) 'Exactly a tenth of produce' applies the tithe law (Deuteronomy 14) to the pilgrimage feasts (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 16:21-22, what were the Israelites forbidden to set up beside the altar of the LORD their God?
options: An Asherah pole or any wooden pillar as an idol
A second altar for burnt offerings
A stone chest inscribed with the names of the patriarchs
A tall tree to hang lamps to light the sanctuary
explanation: Deuteronomy 16:21-22 (ESV): 'You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make. And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.' The correct answer is 'an Asherah pole or wooden pillar as an idol.' (1) 'A second altar for burnt offerings' is a worship violation but is not the prohibition stated here (true_but_off). (2) 'A stone chest inscribed with the names of the patriarchs' is not the forbidden object in this passage (wrong_detail). (3) 'A tall tree to hang lamps' misunderstands the nature of the Asherah tree as an object of pagan worship (common_misconception).

content: According to Deuteronomy 17:6-7, what requirements does the text set regarding witnesses and the carrying out of execution for someone guilty of worshiping other gods?
options: At least two or three witnesses are required, and all the people must act together at once, no one going first
Only one credible witness is needed, and the priest must strike first
At least two or three witnesses are required, and the witnesses must cast the first stone
A confession from the accused is required, and the judge must strike first
explanation: Deuteronomy 17:6-7 (ESV): 'On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death... The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people.' The correct answer combines both details accurately. (1) 'Only one witness... the priest strikes first' is wrong both in number (v.6 requires two or three) and in who strikes first (wrong_detail, almost-right). (2) 'Two or three witnesses... all the people act together at once' gets the witness count right but reverses the order — the text requires the witnesses to strike FIRST, then the rest of the people follow (wrong_detail, almost-right). (3) 'A confession from the accused' imports a modern procedural concept that directly contradicts the witness principle (common_misconception).

content: According to Deuteronomy 17:18-20, why must the king of Israel copy out the law for himself and read it all the days of his life?
options: So that the king may have a long life and expand his territory by knowing the law
So that the king may have authority to amend the law to fit the needs of his era
So that the king may teach the law to the judges and priests of the land
So that the king may fear the LORD, keep the law, and not be proud above his brothers
explanation: Deuteronomy 17:19-20 (ESV): the king must read the law all his days 'that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left.' The correct answer captures the core purpose: fearing the LORD, keeping the law, and not being lifted up above his brothers. (1) 'Long life and expanded territory' takes a secondary promise (v.20 does promise a long reign) as the core purpose, inverting the order of priorities (true_but_off, almost-right). (2) 'Teaching the law to judges and priests' is a worthy action but is not the purpose stated in the text (wrong_scope). (3) 'Authority to amend the law' directly contradicts the command not to 'turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left' (common_misconception).

content: According to Deuteronomy 18:1-2, why does the tribe of Levi receive no inheritance of land like the other tribes?
options: Because the LORD himself is their inheritance
Because they must be scattered among the tribes to teach the law
Because they sinned and were stripped of the right to an inheritance
Because they receive only the cities of refuge in place of farmland
explanation:
Deuteronomy 18:1-2 (ESV) states: 'The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel... They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.' Therefore the correct answer is 'the LORD himself is their inheritance.'
- 'Because they sinned and were stripped of the right to an inheritance' reflects a common misconception (common_misconception): having no territorial inheritance was a privilege of being set apart for the LORD, not a punishment.
- 'Because they must be scattered among the tribes to teach the law' is true of the Levites elsewhere but is not the reason given in this text (true_but_off): verse 2 states the reason directly — the LORD is their inheritance.
- 'Because they receive only the cities of refuge' confuses details: the cities of refuge belong to a different law (ch. 19) and are not described as the Levites' portion in place of an inheritance (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 18:3, when the people offer an ox or a sheep as a sacrifice, which portions are given to the priest?
options: The right thigh and the fat surrounding the entrails
The shoulder, the two cheeks, and the stomach (maw)
The hide and all the blood of the sacrificial animal
The breast that is waved before the LORD
explanation:
Deuteronomy 18:3 (ESV) specifies the priests' due from the people when they offer an ox or a sheep: 'they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach.' That is the correct answer.
- 'The right thigh and the fat surrounding the entrails' are details from the sacrificial laws in Leviticus (e.g., Lev. 7) and are not the portions listed in Deuteronomy 18:3 (near_passage).
- 'The hide and all the blood' is wrong in detail: the blood must be poured out to the LORD and does not belong to the priest (wrong_detail).
- 'The breast that is waved' is a different portion in the offering ritual (Lev. 7:30-31), not the three portions enumerated in Deuteronomy 18:3 (near_passage).

content: In the list of Canaanite abominations prohibited in Deuteronomy 18:10-11, which practice involves children?
options: Forcing one's son to serve for life in a pagan temple
Making one's son or daughter pass through fire
Selling children to foreigners in exchange for idols
Offering the firstborn as a grain offering to Baal
explanation:
Deuteronomy 18:10 opens the list of prohibitions: 'There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering...' followed by divination, sorcery, mediums, and necromancers. Therefore the practice involving children is 'making one's son or daughter pass through fire.'
- 'Forcing one's son to serve for life in a pagan temple' is a fabricated detail not found in the list (wrong_detail).
- 'Offering the firstborn as a grain offering to Baal' mixes elements of grain offerings (which involve grain, not people) with a different deity's name — incorrect detail (wrong_detail).
- 'Selling children to foreigners in exchange for idols' is a practice not mentioned in this passage (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 18:14-15, why were the Israelites not to follow diviners and mediums as the other nations did?
options: Because those diviners were deceivers who never told the truth
Because only the priests were permitted to cast the Urim and Thummim
Because consulting the future has no effect whatsoever
Because the LORD would raise up a prophet for them to reveal His will
explanation:
Deuteronomy 18:14-15: 'the nations...listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this. The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers — it is to him you shall listen.' The reason stated in the text is that the LORD will raise up a prophet to reveal His will, so the people have no need for diviners.
- 'Because the diviners are deceivers' is morally true in general but is not the reason stated in this text (true_but_off).
- 'Only priests may cast the Urim and Thummim' is a true detail from another law (Exodus 28) but is not the reason given in this passage (near_passage).
- 'Consulting the future has no effect' reflects a modern argument rather than the theological reason of verse 15 (common_misconception).

content: What example does Deuteronomy 19:5 use to illustrate the case of a manslayer who may flee to a city of refuge?
options: A man who goes into the forest to cut wood with his neighbor, and the axe head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor dead
A shepherd who swings his staff to drive away a wild animal but accidentally strikes another shepherd
A farmer whose ox gores a passerby to death without his knowledge
A man who climbs onto a roof to make repairs and falls, crushing the person below
explanation:
Deuteronomy 19:5 gives the example of a manslayer: 'as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies...' That is the correct answer.
- 'Swinging a staff to drive away a wild animal' is a fabricated scenario not found in the text (wrong_detail).
- 'An ox goring someone to death' belongs to a different law about a goring ox (Exodus 21:28-29), not the example given here (near_passage).
- 'Climbing a roof and falling' is confused with the law requiring a parapet on a roof (Deuteronomy 22:8), not the axe-head example (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 19:6, why did the law require the cities of refuge to be close enough for a manslayer to reach in time?
options: So that the elders of the city could investigate the case before nightfall
So that the victim's family would have time to calm their anger and forgive
So that the priest could offer an atoning sacrifice for the manslayer
So that the avenger of blood, in his anger, could not overtake and kill an innocent person
explanation:
Deuteronomy 19:6: '...lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die...' The reason is so that the avenger of blood cannot overtake and kill an innocent person. That is the correct answer.
- 'So the elders can investigate before nightfall' adds a time detail not found in the text (wrong_detail).
- 'So the victim's family can calm down and forgive' sounds reasonable but is not the reason stated in verse 6 (true_but_off).
- 'So the priest can offer an atoning sacrifice' misapplies the scope: the city of refuge is a legal sanctuary, not connected to atoning sacrifices here (wrong_scope).

content: What does Deuteronomy 19:14 prohibit the Israelites from doing regarding their neighbor's land boundary?
options: Buying back land from the poor during the Sabbath year
Plowing right up to the edge so that the neighbor's land erodes
Renting out ancestral land to foreigners
Moving the boundary marker that their ancestors had set
explanation:
Deuteronomy 19:14: 'You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold...' The correct answer is 'moving the boundary marker that their ancestors had set.'
- 'Buying back land from the poor during the Sabbath year' is confused with the law of the jubilee and land redemption (Leviticus 25), not the prohibition here (near_passage).
- 'Renting out ancestral land to foreigners' is a detail not present in this verse (wrong_scope).
- 'Plowing right up to the edge causing erosion' sounds related to boundaries but is not the prohibited act in the text (the prohibition is MOVING the marker) (wrong_detail).

content: When a witness is examined and found to have testified falsely, what principle does Deuteronomy 19:18-19 prescribe as punishment?
options: Must pay double the damages that the false testimony caused to the defendant
Must be expelled from the community and barred from entering the assembly of the LORD
Must bring a guilt offering and then publicly apologize before the elders
Must suffer the very punishment he intended to impose on his brother
explanation:
Deuteronomy 19:18-19 (ESV): 'if the witness is a false witness… then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.' The principle is that the false witness must suffer the very punishment he intended to impose on another (connected to 'eye for eye' in verse 21). That is the correct answer.
- 'Pay double the damages' is the principle of restitution in theft law (Exodus 22), not the penalty for false testimony (near_passage); this is an almost-right distractor because it is also an Old Testament legal principle.
- 'Expelled from the community and barred from the assembly' sounds proportionately severe but is not the punishment the text specifies (wrong_detail); almost-right because it seems to match the gravity of the offense.
- 'Bring a guilt offering and apologize' misapplies the scope: false testimony is handled by the law of proportional retribution, not by voluntary offerings (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 20:5-7, which category of person did the officers permit to return home before going to battle?
options: A man who had just been chosen as an elder but had not yet taken office
A man who was betrothed but had not yet held the wedding ceremony
A man who had just built a new house but had not yet dedicated it
A man who had just purchased a herd of livestock but had not yet counted them
explanation:
Deuteronomy 20:5-7 (ESV) lists those the officers send home: (v. 5) the man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it; (v. 6) the man who has planted a vineyard and has not yet enjoyed its fruit; (v. 7) the man who has betrothed a wife and has not yet taken her. The correct answer is 'a man who had just built a new house but had not yet dedicated it.'
- 'A man who had just purchased livestock' is not among the three cases listed (wrong_detail).
- 'A man who was betrothed but had not yet married' IS actually in verse 7 — this is a very tricky almost-right distractor; but the question asks for the person matching the description 'just built a new house and not yet dedicated it,' so the 'built a new house' option (the correct answer) is the true focus, while 'betrothed' is true but phrased here as 'held the wedding ceremony,' placed beside the correct answer to test careful readers (true_but_off relative to the new house description).
- 'A man who had just been chosen as an elder' is a fabricated detail, not found in the list (wrong_scope).

content: When besieging a city for a long time, what kind of tree does Deuteronomy 20:19 forbid the Israelites from cutting down, and what reason does it give?
options: Grapevines, because wine belongs to the drink offerings poured out to the LORD
Olive trees, because their oil is used to anoint kings and priests
Fruit trees, because the trees of the field are not men to be besieged
Cedar trees, because that wood is reserved exclusively for building the temple
explanation:
Deuteronomy 20:19 (ESV): 'When you besiege a city… you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?' The prohibition targets FRUIT trees, with the reason that a tree is not an enemy to be besieged. That is the correct answer.
- 'Olive trees, because oil is used to anoint kings and priests' names a specific tree and gives a different reason (anointing) that is not the reason stated in verse 19; this is almost-right because olive trees are also fruit trees (wrong_detail).
- 'Grapevines, because wine belongs to the drink offerings' are also truly fruit-bearing but the drink-offering reason is not the reason given in the text (true_but_off); almost-right.
- 'Cedar trees for building the temple' is out of scope: cedar is not a fruit tree and the temple reason has nothing to do with verse 19 (wrong_scope).

content: According to Deuteronomy 21:15-17, if a man has two wives and the firstborn son belongs to the unloved wife, how must the man distribute his inheritance?
options: Give the firstborn slightly more than the other sons
Divide the inheritance equally among all sons, without regard to birth order
Transfer the firstborn's rights to the son of the beloved wife
Acknowledge that firstborn son and give him a double portion of his estate
explanation: Deuteronomy 21:17 (ESV): '…he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength.' (1) 'Divide equally among all sons' gets the detail wrong — the law affirms the firstborn's right to a double portion (wrong_detail). (2) 'Transfer the right to the son of the beloved wife' reverses the very thing the law forbids: a man may not, out of favoritism, deprive the true firstborn of his rights (wrong_detail). (3) 'Slightly more' vaguely softens the specific figure 'double portion' (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 22:8, when building a new house, what must an Israelite do for the roof?
options: Plant shade trees so the roof will not crack from the sun
Build a parapet around the roof
Erect a small altar to offer firstfruits offerings
Coat it with white lime to mark the house as set apart
explanation: Deuteronomy 22:8 (ESV): 'When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it.' The parapet is to prevent fatal accidents. (1) 'Plant shade trees' completely misses the safety purpose (wrong_detail). (2) 'Erect an altar on the roof' is an idolatrous practice condemned elsewhere in the law, not this command (wrong_scope). (3) 'Coat it with white lime' has no basis in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 25:1-3, when a guilty person is sentenced to be flogged, what is the maximum number of lashes permitted?
options: Seven lashes
Ten lashes for each offense committed
At the judge's discretion, with no limit
Forty lashes
explanation: Deuteronomy 25:3: 'Forty lashes may be given him, but not more, lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, your brother be degraded in your sight.' The limit was designed to protect the dignity of the one being punished. (1) 'Seven lashes' gives the wrong number (wrong_detail). (2) 'Ten lashes per offense' introduces a multiplying mechanism not found in the law (wrong_detail). (3) 'No limit' denies the very purpose of the law, which was to set a maximum (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 25:13-16, what is 'an abomination to the LORD' concerning trade and commerce?
options: Trading with the foreign nations living around their borders
Selling goods and grain on the Sabbath set apart as holy
Lending money at interest to a poor brother in need
Having in your bag two kinds of weights and two kinds of measures, both large and small
explanation: Deuteronomy 25:13-16 forbids having 'two kinds of weights... two kinds of measures' in your bag, and verse 16 declares that 'all who act dishonestly are an abomination to the LORD your God.' This concerns fraudulent measurement. (1) 'Trading with foreign nations' is not what is prohibited in this passage (wrong_detail). (2) 'Lending at interest' belongs to a different law (23:19-20), not this passage (near_passage). (3) 'Selling on the Sabbath' shifts to Sabbath law and does not belong to the weights-and-measures passage (near_passage).

content: According to Deuteronomy 21:1-9, when a slain body is found in the open country and the killer is unknown, what must the elders of the nearest city do to make atonement for the bloodshed?
options: Offer a male lamb as a sin offering at the place where the body was found
Cast lots among the neighboring towns to determine who bears responsibility for the bloodshed
Break the neck of a heifer that has never been worked at a valley with running water, then wash their hands and declare their innocence
Bring the body back to the city and bury it with a communal mourning ritual for seven days
explanation: Deuteronomy 21:4-7: the elders brought 'a heifer that has never been worked... to a valley with running water... and shall break the heifer's neck there,' then washed their hands over the heifer and declared, 'Our hands did not shed this blood.' (1) 'A male lamb as a sin offering' substitutes the wrong animal and the wrong rite — the text specifies a heifer whose neck is broken, not a regular sacrifice (wrong_detail). (2) 'Casting lots to find the perpetrator' has no place in this ritual; the purpose is communal atonement when the killer is unknown (wrong_detail). (3) 'Seven days of mourning' imports details from a different law and does not belong to the heifer rite (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 21:10-13, if a man desires to marry a beautiful captive woman, what must she first be allowed to do?
options: Offer a burnt offering to be cleansed from the defilement of foreign peoples
Shave her head, pare her nails, and mourn her father and mother for a full month
Learn the law of Israel for seven days before the marriage
Return to visit her family one last time before the wedding
explanation: Deuteronomy 21:12-13: '...she shall shave her head and pare her nails. And she shall take off the clothes she captured in... and she shall lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife.' (1) 'Offer a burnt offering for cleansing' is not found in this passage; the rite is a transitional mourning period, not a sacrifice (wrong_detail). (2) 'Learn the law for seven days' is a fabricated detail, wrong in both content and duration — the text specifies one month, not seven days (wrong_detail). (3) 'Return to visit her family' is contradictory — she is mourning her own parents while already in her husband's household (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 23:15-16, when a slave escapes from his master and seeks refuge, how must an Israelite treat him?
options: Keep him as their own slave until the Year of Jubilee
Return him to his former master to maintain social order
Bring him before the elders to judge his act of running away
Do not hand him over to his master; let him dwell wherever he chooses among you, and do not oppress him
explanation: Deuteronomy 23:15-16: 'You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose... You shall not wrong him.' The law protects the one who has fled. (1) 'Keep him as a slave until the Year of Jubilee' turns the place of refuge into a new form of servitude, contrary to the spirit of the law (wrong_detail). (2) 'Return him to his former master' is precisely what the law explicitly forbids (common_misconception — a natural 'social order' reflex). (3) 'Bring him before the elders for judgment' adds a procedure not found in the text and implies the fugitive is guilty (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 24:6, why does the law forbid taking a millstone (or its upper stone) as a pledge?
options: Because doing so is like taking a person's very life
Because the millstone is a sacred object used only for grain offerings
Because the millstone is too heavy to carry as a valid pledge
Because the millstone belongs to the whole family, not to one individual
explanation: Deuteronomy 24:6: 'No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge, for that would be taking a life in pledge.' The millstone was the means of making daily bread; seizing it strips away a neighbor's livelihood. (1) 'A sacred object for grain offerings' sounds plausible but the text gives a humanitarian reason, not a ceremonial one (true_but_off). (2) 'Too heavy to carry' is a practical reason that does not match the text's stated rationale (wrong_detail). (3) 'Belongs to the whole family' invents a collective-ownership reason not found in the verse (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 23:3–8, how does the law distinguish between the Ammonites/Moabites and the Edomites/Egyptians regarding entry into the assembly of the LORD?
options: Ammonites and Moabites are excluded until the tenth generation; Edomites and Egyptians may be admitted from the third generation
All four nations are excluded forever, with no exceptions
Ammonites and Moabites may be admitted from the third generation; Edomites and Egyptians are excluded until the tenth generation
Ammonites and Moabites are excluded forever; Edomites and Egyptians may be admitted from the tenth generation
explanation: Deuteronomy 23:3 excludes Ammonites and Moabites 'to the tenth generation... forever' (because they did not meet Israel with bread and water and hired Balaam against them), while 23:7–8 says 'You shall not abhor an Edomite... You shall not abhor an Egyptian... Children born to them in the third generation may enter the assembly of the LORD.' (1) 'All four nations excluded forever' erases the core distinction of the passage (wrong_scope). (2) Reverses the two groups — assigns the third generation to Ammon/Moab (wrong_detail, almost-right). (3) Assigns the tenth generation to Edom/Egypt — the right number applied to the wrong group (wrong_detail, almost-right).

content: In the law about a rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:18–21, who brings him before the elders, and what is the ultimate purpose of the punishment?
options: The city judge arrests him, and the purpose is to require him to make restitution for all harm done to the community
The priest leads him away, and the purpose is to offer him as a sacrifice to atone for the sins of his parents' household
Both father and mother bring him out, and the purpose is to 'purge the evil from your midst' so that all Israel will hear and fear
The father alone accuses him, and the purpose is to strip him of his entire inheritance
explanation: Deuteronomy 21:19–21: 'his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city,' the men of the city shall stone him to death, 'so you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.' Both parents must testify, and the purpose is collective deterrence. (1) 'The city judge arrests him... restitution' is wrong on both the agent and the purpose — the penalty is death, not financial restitution (wrong_detail). (2) 'The priest leads him away... atoning sacrifice' turns a judicial execution into a cultic rite (wrong_scope). (3) 'The father alone... strip inheritance' is half right about the father's role but omits the mother and reduces the death penalty to mere forfeiture of property (wrong_detail, almost-right).

content: According to Deuteronomy 26:12, the tithe of the third year (the year of tithing) is set aside to provide for whom?
options: The priests serving at the temple
The Levites, sojourners, orphans, and widows
The elders and judges of the city
The soldiers going out to battle to defend the people
explanation: Deuteronomy 26:12 teaches that in the third year, the year of tithing, the people must give to 'the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow' so that they may eat their fill in your towns — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'The priests serving at the temple' is wrong in detail: the third-year tithe is stored in the towns for the poor, not directed specifically to the priests (wrong_detail). (2) 'The elders and judges' are not among those named — they are administrators of justice, not beneficiaries (wrong_scope). (3) 'Soldiers going out to battle' is a detail entirely foreign to this tithing law (wrong_detail).

content: In Deuteronomy 26:17–19, what does the 'today' declaration between the LORD and Israel confirm about their relationship?
options: Israel promises to offer all firstfruits, and the LORD promises to send rain and favorable weather
Israel declares the LORD to be their God, and the LORD declares them to be his treasured people
The LORD appoints Moses as king, and the people promise to obey all his commands
The LORD promises to forgive all sins committed in the wilderness if the people agree to be circumcised
explanation: Deuteronomy 26:17–19: the people 'have declared today that the LORD is your God,' and the LORD declares today that Israel is 'his treasured possession' and that he will set them high above all nations — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'Offer firstfruits... rain and favorable weather' blends in nearby content (26:1–11 on firstfruits) but is not the focus of this covenant declaration (near_passage). (2) 'Appointing Moses as king' misidentifies the scope: the covenant is between the LORD and the people, and no king is installed here (wrong_scope). (3) 'Forgive sins if circumcised' is a fabricated detail not found in this declaration (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 27:2-4, after crossing the Jordan River into the promised land, the people were required to set up large stones and do what with them?
options: Engrave the names of the twelve tribes of Israel on each stone
Pour oil on them as memorial pillars to commemorate the crossing of the Jordan
Stack them into twelve heaps corresponding to the number of days the people marched around
Plaster them with plaster and write on them all the words of this law
explanation: RVV11 Deuteronomy 27:2-4: the people were to set up large stones, 'plaster them with plaster' and 'write on them all the words of this law' — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'Engrave the names of the twelve tribes' is an incorrect detail: the stones were for writing the law, not for engraving tribal names (wrong_detail). (2) 'Pour oil as memorial pillars' confuses this with actions of the patriarchs (such as Jacob at Bethel), not the command given here (near_passage). (3) 'Twelve heaps corresponding to the number of days of marching' mixes in the later account in Joshua at Jericho, which is not this command (wrong_detail).

content: Deuteronomy 27:5-6 specifies that the altar built for the LORD must be made of what kind of stone, and where is the reason found?
options: Dressed stones, precisely cut and fitted together so the altar would be sturdy
Whole stones, untouched by any iron tool
Stones overlaid with pure gold to be worthy of offering to God
White stones taken from the bed of the Jordan River they had just crossed
explanation: RVV11 Deuteronomy 27:5-6: 'You shall not wield an iron tool on them'; the altar must be built of 'whole stones' — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'Dressed stones, precisely cut' is almost right but directly contradicts the command: the altar must use stones that have not been cut or dressed (wrong_detail). (2) 'White stones taken from the bed of the Jordan' mixes in details about the stones taken from the Jordan, not the material for the altar (near_passage). (3) 'Stones overlaid with gold' confuses this with the ornamentation of the tabernacle and temple, which does not apply to this stone altar (wrong_scope).

content: In the series of curses in Deuteronomy 28:23-24, if the people are disobedient, what will the sky above them and the earth beneath them become?
options: The sky will be pitch dark all day, and the earth will crack open and swallow the harvest
The sky will rain hail and fire, and the earth will produce thorns instead of wheat
The sky will be like bronze and the earth like iron; the rain will turn to dust and powder
The sky will blot out the sun, the earth will tremble, and houses will collapse
explanation: RVV11 Deuteronomy 28:23-24: 'And the heavens over your head shall be bronze, and the earth under you shall be iron'; the LORD will make the rain of your land become 'powder and dust' — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'The sky pitch dark… the earth cracking open' sounds fitting for a curse context but is not the language used here (wrong_detail). (2) 'Hail and fire… thorns' mixes imagery from the plagues of Egypt and Genesis 3, not this verse (near_passage). (3) 'Blotting out the sun… trembling' is the imagery of the day of judgment in the prophetic books, out of context for this curse passage (true_but_off).

content: Deuteronomy 28:68 describes the climax of the curses when the people are scattered: the LORD will bring them back to Egypt by ship, and there they will offer to sell themselves as what — and what will be the outcome?
options: Sell themselves as slaves, and be forced to labor building cities for Pharaoh
Sell their children as slaves in order to buy back their own freedom
Sell themselves as mercenary soldiers, and die in a foreign land
Offer themselves for sale as slaves, but no one will buy them
explanation: RVV11 Deuteronomy 28:68: the LORD will bring the people back to Egypt by ship, and there 'you shall offer yourselves for sale to your enemies as male and female slaves, but there will be no buyer' — the correct answer is option 0; the tragedy is that even the status of a slave is something no one will purchase. (1) 'Labor building cities for Pharaoh' evokes the initial bondage in Exodus, not the language here (near_passage). (2) 'Sell their children to buy back their own freedom' reverses the meaning: they themselves offer to sell themselves and find no buyer — it is not about selling children (wrong_detail). (3) 'Sell themselves as mercenary soldiers' is a fabricated detail not found in this verse (wrong_detail).

content: In Deuteronomy 29:5, Moses reminds the people of what sign that demonstrated God's care for them throughout forty years in the wilderness?
options: The hair on their heads never turned gray despite the passing of years
Their clothing did not wear out and the sandals on their feet did not wear out
The food in their storehouses never ran out
Their weapons never rusted or were damaged
explanation: RVV11 Deuteronomy 29:5: 'Your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet' throughout forty years — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'Hair never turning gray' is a fabricated sign not found in this verse (wrong_detail). (2) 'Food in the storehouses never running out' confuses this with the miracle of manna (Exodus 16), not the language here (near_passage). (3) 'Weapons never rusting' is a detail not mentioned at all (wrong_detail).

content: Deuteronomy 31:9-13: Moses wrote down the law and commanded that it be read aloud to all the people. At what interval and on what feast was this to occur?
options: At the end of every seven years, in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths
At the end of every seven years, in the Year of Jubilee, at the Feast of Passover
On the first of every month, on the day of the new moon, before the ark of the covenant
Once every year, on the great Day of Atonement at the sanctuary
explanation: Deuteronomy 31:10-11: 'at the end of every seven years, at the set time in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths,' this law is to be read before all Israel — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'Every year… Day of Atonement' is wrong in both the cycle and the feast: the interval is seven years and the feast is Booths (wrong_detail). (2) 'Year of Jubilee… Feast of Passover' preserves the seven-year cycle but changes both the name of the year and the feast (Passover instead of Booths) — almost correct but wrong on two key details (wrong_detail). (3) 'Every month… new moon' is a fabricated detail that confuses this passage with other periodic liturgical rites (wrong_detail).
tags: Reading the law every seven years

content: In the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:35), what does the LORD declare belongs to Him concerning the enemies of His people?
options: The judgment of all nations belongs to Me, for I made all things
Vengeance is Mine, and recompense; their foot shall slip in due time
The redemption of My people belongs to Me, not by sword or spear of man
Forgiveness and mercy belong to Me forever
explanation: Deuteronomy 32:35: 'Vengeance is mine, and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip' — the correct answer is option 1. (1) 'The judgment of all nations… I made all things' is true of God in general but is not what is declared in this verse (true_but_off). (2) 'Redemption… not by sword or spear' reflects a theme found elsewhere in the Song and in the Psalms, straying from verse 35 (near_passage). (3) 'Forgiveness and mercy' inverts the focus: this verse speaks of retribution against enemies, not mercy (wrong_detail).

content: According to Deuteronomy 34:9, why did the people of Israel obey Joshua after the death of Moses?
options: Because Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him
Because Joshua was the only one still alive who had come out of Egypt with Moses
Because the LORD appeared in a pillar of cloud and appointed Joshua before the whole congregation
Because Joshua was from the tribe of Levi and therefore had the right to succeed as leader of the people
explanation: Deuteronomy 34:9: Joshua 'was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him,' so the people obeyed him — the correct answer is option 0. (1) 'The only one still alive who came out of Egypt' is wrong: Caleb also survived, and the verse does not give this as the reason (wrong_detail). (2) 'The LORD appeared in a pillar of cloud' confuses this with the commissioning of Joshua in 31:14-15, not verse 34:9 (near_passage). (3) 'From the tribe of Levi' is factually wrong: Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim, not Levi (wrong_scope).
